notes.meaning: Elijah and Elisha set out from Gilgal on Elijah's final journey. God had made it known that He was about to take Elijah bodily into heaven in a whirlwind. This great event showed God's people that there is real life with Him beyond this world.

Elijah urged Elisha to stay behind while he traveled on to Bethel. Elisha made a solemn vow by the living Lord that he would never leave his master. This tested Elisha's devotion and proved that he was fully committed to his teacher.

Student prophets at Bethel came out and asked Elisha if he knew his master was being taken that day. Elisha told them he already knew and asked them to be quiet about it. He felt deep grief over Elijah's departure and preferred quiet reverence over chatter.

Elijah asked Elisha again to stay behind while he went on to Jericho. Elisha gave the exact same answer, swearing by God that he would not leave his side. His persistence showed his readiness to walk with his mentor to the very end.

The student prophets at Jericho came to Elisha with the same question about Elijah's departure. Elisha gave his same reply, telling them he knew and asking them to keep peaceful silence. God had revealed the coming event to all of them, but Elisha was focused on his master's final hours.

For a third time, Elijah told Elisha to stay behind as he went on toward the Jordan River. Elisha repeated his solemn oath that he would stay by Elijah, and the two walked on together. True faithfulness means staying close to God's work even when separation is near.

Fifty men from the company of prophets followed them and stood watching from a distance by the Jordan. They were not allowed to go with them, but they watched to see how they would cross. Their watchful eyes provided reliable witnesses for what God was about to do.

Elijah took his prophet's cloak, rolled it up, and struck the Jordan River with it. The waters parted to both sides, and the two prophets walked across on dry ground. Just as God opened the sea for Moses and the river for Joshua, He showed that His power was fully active through Elijah.

After crossing, Elijah invited Elisha to make a final request before they were parted. Elisha asked for a double portion of Elijah's spirit. Under Israel's law, the firstborn son received a double share of the inheritance, so Elisha was asking to be recognized as Elijah's true spiritual successor.

Elijah answered that Elisha had asked for a difficult blessing, because only God can give spiritual gifts. He gave Elisha a sign: if Elisha was permitted to see him taken away, the request would be granted. This kept Elisha watching closely and trusting God to give the blessing.

While they walked and talked, a chariot of fire and horses of fire suddenly drove between the two men. Elijah was then carried up into heaven by a whirlwind without dying. God gave a glorious display of His heavenly army as He welcomed His servant home.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars view the chariot and horses of fire as poetic Hebrew imagery describing God's majesty in a powerful storm rather than a literal vehicle.

notes.meaning: Elisha saw the whole event and cried out that Elijah was like the chariots and horsemen of Israel. He meant that one faithful prophet had protected the nation more than any earthly army. Overcome with grief at losing his spiritual father, Elisha tore his own clothes in two.

Elisha picked up the prophet's cloak that had fallen from Elijah as he ascended. He then turned back and stood alone on the bank of the Jordan River. Taking up the cloak was an outward sign that he accepted the call to continue Elijah's ministry.

Elisha struck the water with Elijah's cloak and called upon the Lord, the God of Elijah. The waters divided once again, and Elisha crossed over on dry ground. This showed that the power belonged to God alone and that the Lord was now working through Elisha.

The prophets from Jericho saw the miracle and knew that Elijah's spirit now rested upon Elisha. They went out to meet him and bowed down before him with deep respect. They gladly accepted him as their new leader because God had clearly placed His authority on him.

The prophets suggested sending fifty strong men to search the mountains and valleys for Elijah. They worried that the Spirit of the Lord might have carried him away and dropped him somewhere in the wilderness. Elisha told them not to go, knowing that Elijah had truly been taken to heaven.

The men kept urging Elisha until he was embarrassed to keep refusing, so he allowed them to send the search party. Fifty men searched for three days but found nothing. This search gave clear proof that Elijah was truly gone and had not simply wandered away.

When the searchers returned empty-handed to Jericho, Elisha reminded them that he had told them not to go. His words showed that his prophetic guidance was completely trustworthy. Listening to God's word saves us from pointless effort.

The men of Jericho told Elisha that while their city was in a pleasant spot, the water was bad and the land was unfruitful. The unhealthy spring was causing plants to fail and animals to miscarry. They turned to God's prophet to solve a real community problem.

Elisha told them to bring a brand new bowl and put salt in it. The bowl had to be new because holy service required an instrument that was clean and unused. The salt served as an outward symbol of purity and preservation.

Elisha went straight to the natural spring and threw the salt into the water. He declared in the name of the Lord that God had healed the water so it would no longer cause death or barrenness. The healing was an act of God's power, not the natural effect of the salt.

The water became fresh and wholesome, just as Elisha had promised by the word of the Lord. The blessing remained for generations to come, bringing life and health to the city. What the Lord heals remains healed.

Elisha traveled up toward Bethel, which was a known center for calf worship and idolatry. On the way, a large group of youths came out of the city and mocked him, shouting for him to go up and calling him baldhead. By chanting for him to go up, they were mocking Elijah's ascension and scorning God's new prophet.

Elisha turned and spoke a curse over the mockers in the name of the Lord. Suddenly two female bears came out of the woods and mauled forty-two of the young men. God acted to defend the honor of His prophet and to warn the nation against mocking His holy word.

Elisha left Bethel and traveled to Mount Carmel, and from there he went on to Samaria. Carmel was a quiet place where Elijah had often prayed, giving Elisha time to prepare for his work. After that time of preparation, he entered the capital city to begin his public ministry.
